big_idea: We can use the rule to find missing animals anywhere in the parade and to explain — out loud — why our prediction is right.
learning_intention: We are learning to find missing elements in repeating patterns and to justify our predictions using the rule.
student_learning_goal: I can find a missing animal and tell my partner why I am sure.
success_criteria: I can find a missing animal at the start, middle, OR end of a parade.
I can use the rule to explain why my answer is right.
I can extend a parade forward AND backward using the rule.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart from previous lessons (PATTERN, CORE, RULE up; add MISSING and EXTEND from M6 today; hand-print JUSTIFY beside them)

Three pre-built broken parade strips for the opening reveal: one with a missing middle (Bea-Finn-?-Bea-Finn), one with a missing end (Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-?), one with a missing START (?-Finn-Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn)
MISSING and EXTEND word cards (M6) ready to tape on the chart
Class formative tracker for Lesson 4 (provided in assessment_suite stage)

minds_on.hook: Coco needs detectives! Three of his parades have animals MISSING — at the start, the middle, or the end. Can we crack the case?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lay the three broken strips in a row, each with a Missing Mystery Card (M4) in the gap.

Say to students: 'Friends, big problem. Coco's parades have GAPS. One has a missing animal in the MIDDLE, one at the END, one at the START. We are detectives today. Our job is to figure out who is missing AND, the Grade 1 rule, JUSTIFY — that means TELL me HOW we know.' Tape the JUSTIFY card hand-printed on chart paper. 'Justify means: give a reason. We are not just guessing. We use the RULE.'

Point to Strip 1 (missing middle): Bea-Finn-?-Bea-Finn. 'Look. Whose card is in the gap?' Take predictions. Push: 'How do you KNOW?' Listen for: 'because the rule is AB, and after Bea comes Finn'. Validate.

Quickly walk through Strip 2 (missing end) and Strip 3 (missing start). The missing-start case is the hardest — children must extend BACKWARD using the rule. Reassure that backward thinking is detective thinking.
student_actions: Sit in a circle on the carpet.
Predict the missing animal in each broken parade.
Practice using the sentence frame: 'I think it is ___ because the rule is ___.'
Repeat the new word 'justify' aloud as a class.

action.activity_name: Detectives at Work — Fix and Extend

steps.instruction: Whole group demo: take a clean strip and build Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn-?-? leaving the last two cells empty. Say: 'Two animals missing at the end. Find the rule first, then fill the gaps.' Take predictions and justifications. Then: 'Now I am adding ?-?-Bea-Finn-Finn at the START. Find what came BEFORE.' Walk children through using the rule to extend backward. Emphasize: same rule, just running it backward.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Detectives — first the rule, then the gap. Always. The rule is your magnifying glass.' Model the sentence: 'The rule is ABB, so cell 7 is Bea, and cell 8 is Finn, because after Finn-Finn the rule starts over with Bea.'

steps.instruction: Send children to partner spots. Each pair gets Animal Cards (M1), one Parade Strip (M2), 5 Missing Mystery Cards (M4), and one Core Loop Frame (M5). The first child builds a broken parade (must include at least one Missing Card somewhere — start, middle, or end). The second child plays detective: identifies the rule, fills the gap, and justifies aloud. Then they swap.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Partner A: build a broken parade. You pick the rule. Hide one or two animals using Missing Cards. Partner B: find the rule first, then fill the gap, then JUSTIFY out loud. Swap. The detective who can SAY HOW THEY KNOW gets a high five from Coco.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge: pairs exchange parades with another pair. Each pair now has a stranger's broken parade. They must extend it BOTH directions — add 2 cells at the start AND 2 cells at the end — using the rule. This combines find-the-missing with extend-both-ways.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Time to swap with another pair. Now the parade is from a stranger! Find the rule, fix any gaps, and add TWO cells at the front and TWO cells at the back. Show your work to the pair who built it. They have to agree the rule is right.'

steps.instruction: Circulate. Use the formative tracker. Look especially for: did the child JUSTIFY out loud, not just place a card silently? Could they extend backward, not just forward? The tracker columns capture position-of-gap difficulty (start vs middle vs end) because that order reflects difficulty.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Pick one child. Ask: 'How did you know what was missing here?' Then: 'And what would come BEFORE the start of the parade? How do you know?' Record on the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay with AB rules and middle-gaps only. Provide a sentence frame card: 'I think it is ___ because the rule is ___.' Pair with a confident peer who can model the justification first. Accept gestures or pointing to the rule sticker as a valid justification.
differentiation.for_extending: Use ABB, AAB, or ABC rules. Multiple gaps in one parade. Add the requirement: extend the parade 4 cells in both directions. For super-extending pairs, ask: 'If this parade had 20 cells, who would be in cell 20? Use the rule to figure it out without drawing every cell.'
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Use a sentence frame card: 'It is ___. Rule is ___.' Allow the child to point to the rule label on the chart while saying the animal name. Accept any verbal justification, however short. Provide a parade with only ONE missing cell to reduce load.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: After fixing the strip, the pair walks the FULL repaired parade including the extensions, calling out the rule rhythmically. Walking the extension backward (taking 4 steps backward while calling A-B-B in reverse) helps the backward-extension idea stick.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child find a missing element in different positions (start hardest, end easiest)? Can they justify using rule language ('because the rule is ABB')? Can they extend forward AND backward? Do they pick up the rule from a stranger's parade independently?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the appropriate column on the Lesson 4 formative tracker.

discussion_prompts: Who solved a tricky parade today? Tell us the rule and how you knew what was missing.
Was it harder to find the missing animal at the START or at the END? Why do you think that is?
If your parade had 100 cells, could you tell me who would be in cell 100? How would you figure it out?
consolidation.exit_routine: On the way out the door, each child says one full justify sentence: 'I am a Pattern Detective because I can use the rule ___ to find a missing ___.' Teacher nods or quietly redirects.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Class formative tracker for C1.3 (find missing + justify), plus completed student worksheet 'Pattern Detective'.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Justifying predictions is the hard Grade 1 marker — it separates children who simply pattern-match from children who reason with the rule. The teacher needs evidence of who can verbalize the rule-as-reason before Lesson 5 (the summative) requires it formally. The position-of-gap columns reflect known difficulty: middle and end gaps are within reach by Grade 1; start gaps and backward extension often need scaffolding well into Grade 2.

expanded_walkthrough.title: Detective Justification — finding what's missing AND saying why
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: L4's added cognitive demand over K is JUSTIFICATION — children must explain out loud why the missing animal is what they say. The new Grade 1 marker. Step 3 (extending BOTH directions of a stranger's parade) is where strong rule-ownership separates from neighbour-matching. This walkthrough covers the script for the most common stuck moments: extending backward AND justifying the move.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Each pair starts with their own parade-strip rule. By Step 3 they have a stranger's broken parade in front of them. A Core Loop Frame (M5) sits on each table for use as a thinking tool. Sticky notes are nearby for writing the rule. The clipboard tracks 'extends forward,' 'extends backward,' and 'justifies aloud' as separate columns.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Walk to a pair that has identified the stranger's rule and is now extending. Stop them mid-task. 'You just put a Finn at the start. Tell me — why Finn and not Bea?' Wait. Listen for the strong G1 answer: 'Because the rule is AAB. So if I work backwards from cell 3 which is a Finn, the rule going BACKWARD is also AAB, just starting from Finn. So cell 2 is Bea, cell 1 is Bea.' Some children give this answer naturally. Most cannot — they default to 'because Finn was the next one to use,' which is neighbour-thinking, not rule-thinking.

When you hear neighbour-thinking, redirect with the loop. 'Show me the rule with M5 first.' Have them place the loop on the visible cells. 'Now imagine sliding that same loop to the LEFT, off the strip. What animals would be inside?' Some children will see it. Others need you to physically slide a second loop to the left while narrating: 'AAB-AAB-AAB. Three AABs to the left of where we started.'

Now stretch the strong children. Hand them a parade with a missing element in the MIDDLE and ask: 'Don't just fix it. Tell me three different ways someone might JUSTIFY the answer.' Listen for: 'because the rule is AAB and that's where the third B goes,' 'because the parade has to keep the same rule going,' 'because the cell next to it is the start of the next core.' Three justifications for the same answer = full L4 ownership.

Record on the formative clipboard. Justifies-aloud is the column that matters most for the new G1 marker.
expected_student_responses: (Strong) Explains the rule, justifies the extension, articulates direction-independence.
(Mid) Extends correctly forward but fills cells 1-2 in forward order (e.g., Bea-Bea-Finn instead of Finn-Bea-Bea).
(Confused) Says 'I put what felt right' or 'because the next one was Finn.' Neighbour-thinking, not rule-thinking.
(Stretched) Articulates that backward and forward extensions follow the SAME rule applied in different temporal directions.
common_misconceptions: Backward extension reverses the rule. (Child fills 1-2 in the same forward order as 3-4 instead of running the rule backward in time.)
Justification is restating the answer. (Child says 'because it's Bea' rather than 'because the rule is AAB and that position is the second A.')
The rule changes based on where the missing element sits. (Child treats end-extension and middle-fill as different conceptual tasks rather than two applications of the same rule.)
recovery_moves: Slide a second loop physically to the LEFT of the strip. Narrate the rule running backward in time. Make the inversion visible, not just verbal.
Force the WHY. After every placement, ask 'because the rule is…?' If the child finishes 'AAB and that position is the second B,' they own it. Anything else needs more practice.
Compare two missing-element positions. 'Why is the answer at cell 5 different from the answer at cell 1?' Force articulation that BOTH come from the same rule, just applied at different positions.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C1.3 — finding missing elements in different positions, extending in both directions, and justifying predictions using the rule.

parts_outline.task: Show three short broken parades (each 6 cells): one with a missing middle (AB rule), one with a missing end (ABB rule), one with a missing start (ABC rule). Student fills the gap in each AND writes the rule label on a line beside each parade.

Show an 8-cell parade with cells 3-6 filled (Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea), cells 1-2 empty, cells 7-8 empty. Student fills BOTH ends using the rule. Below the parade, a sentence frame: 'The rule is ___. I know cells 1 and 2 are ___ and ___ because ___.'

Detective scenario: 'Coco built a parade. He says cell 5 is Bibi. The rule is AAB. Use the rule to figure out cells 1 through 4 — and cell 6.' A blank 6-cell strip with 'Bibi' written in cell 5. Student fills the other cells. Below: 'I am sure because ___.'

An 8-cell parade strip with a fillable middle and two empty ends
A 6-cell strip with one cell pre-filled (Bibi in cell 5) for Part 3
